extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in mathematical analysis; readers interested in history/philosophy of mathematics (Cauchy, uniform convergence, nonstandard analysis)
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and evaluate conditions under which the pointwise/ uniform/ equicontinuous limit of a sequence of continuous functions is itself continuous, including historical proofs, counterexamples, and nonstandard-analysis interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-theorem (attributed to Cauchy, 1821): pointwise convergence preserves continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f = (f1, f2, …) be an infinite sequence of continuous functions from the real line to itself. Suppose that, for every real number x, the sequence (f1(x), f2(x), …) converges to some real number f_∞(x) (i.e., f converges pointwise to f_∞). Then f_∞ is also continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the original claim attributed to Cauchy but is now regarded as false. The page explains that the claim conflates pointwise and uniform convergence, and gives counterexamples (Fourier series, the sequence fn(x)=x^n on [0,1], fn(x)=exp(-n|x|)) demonstrating the limit need not be continuous when only pointwise convergence is assumed. Historical/philosophical notes: Cauchy denied some counterexamples on the grounds that convergence did not occur everywhere in his sense; Lakatos argued Cauchy's notion may have been closer to uniform convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem (attributed to Seidel, 1847): uniform convergence preserves continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f = (f1, f2, …) be an infinite sequence of continuous functions from the real line to itself. Suppose that the sequence f converges uniformly to a function f_∞. Then f_∞ is also continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard correct theorem. The page gives epsilontic and nonstandard proofs: in epsilontics one chooses N independent of h so that |f_n(x+h)-f_∞(x+h)| and |f_n(x)-f_∞(x)| < ε/3 for all h, and uses continuity of f_n to bound |f_n(x+h)-f_n(x)| < ε/3 when h small; summing yields < ε. The key point is uniform convergence makes the choice of N independent of h.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem: equicontinuity plus pointwise convergence implies continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f = (f1, f2, …) be an equicontinuous sequence of (necessarily continuous) functions from the real line to itself. Suppose that for every real x the sequence (f1(x), f2(x), …) converges to f_∞(x) (pointwise). Then f_∞ is also continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equicontinuity supplies a δ that works for every fn simultaneously, so the usual ε/3 argument can be arranged with n chosen large enough (depending on x but not on which fn) and h small enough to control the middle term. The page presents both epsilontic and nonstandard proofs. Note: the sequence must be equicontinuous (a stronger uniformity condition than mere pointwise convergence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexamples to Cauchy's original claim (illustrative examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit sequences of continuous functions whose pointwise limits are not continuous: the Fourier-series example (sawtooth wave sum ∑ sin(kx)/k), fn(x)=x^n on [0,1], and fn(x)=exp(-n|x|).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each partial sum or fn is continuous, the pointwise limit exists but is discontinuous (e.g., x^n → function that is 0 on [0,1) and 1 at 1). These examples are not equicontinuous and do not converge uniformly; they thus show why pointwise convergence alone cannot guarantee continuity of the limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common flaw in Cauchy's epsilontic argument: illicit dependence of n on h (mixing quantifiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cauchy's argument bounds |f_∞(x+h)-f_∞(x)| by three terms and for each term chooses N or δ potentially depending on h or n; the flaw is treating those choices as if they could be made simultaneously (i.e., letting n depend on h and h depend on n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explicates the epsilontic error using ε/3: the N guaranteeing |f_n(x)-f_∞(x)|<ε/3 may depend on x and h, while the δ for continuity of f_n may depend on n; they cannot be chosen independently without additional uniformity hypotheses. Fixes: require uniform convergence (N independent of h) or equicontinuity (δ independent of n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstandard-analysis critique: misuse of the transfer principle
rubrics_metrics.description: When Cauchy's argument is written in nonstandard-analysis terms, the page warns that the two uses of the transfer principle are illegitimate because the statements to which they are applied are not first-order in the language of the real numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explains the specific failure with examples (e.g., fn(x)=exp(-n|x|)) and shows how a correct nonstandard formulation of uniform convergence/equicontinuity leads to valid nonstandard proofs. It also gives a careful nonstandard reconstruction showing which steps fail and how to correct them by stating appropriate nearstandard/uniform conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/interpretive criterion (Lakatos): 'converges for each variable real number' ≈ uniform convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Lakatos's interpretation: Cauchy said convergence 'for each variable real number' (a variable whose value may depend on n); interpreting this notion makes Cauchy's claim closer to uniform convergence and rescues his theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page discusses Lakatos's view that interpreting convergence in this stronger sense (convergence along every convergent sequence x_n, or for every variable real) is equivalent, given continuity of the f_n, to uniform convergence. Thus historically one may read Cauchy as implicitly assuming a stronger notion of convergence; the page also notes Lakatos later partially re-evaluated this reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correcting Cauchy's proof: two valid fixes (uniform convergence or equicontinuity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two ways to repair the flawed proof: assume uniform convergence of f_n to f_∞, or assume the family {f_n} is equicontinuous and retain only pointwise convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives epsilontic and nonstandard proofs for both fixes, showing precisely how either hypothesis removes the illicit dependence between n and h. This entry synthesizes the corrective methods and connects them to the earlier theorems (Seidel and the equicontinuity theorem).
